finding: the EMITTED ranking differs sharply from the EXECUTED ranking, and it promotes one lever: dsr:x17-materialize is 29.1% of all emitted words -- the largest single class, larger than any guest class -- against 13.9% of sampled executed PCs. Exit-target materialization dominates footprint far more than cycles. The design doc's Phase C already names the fix (load the target from the context or a literal pool instead of a four-word movz/movk chain, as `26de3c07` already did for gateway addresses), and it would cut both footprint and cycles.
corrected: an earlier estimate of 4.1 GB emitted / 14.3% of zfod faults was wrong by 5.1x. `cache_used_bytes` is a PER-THREAD profile frame; summing the frames counts each process's cache once per thread (444 frames, 68 processes). Correct by-pid sum is 812,782,912 bytes and the directly measured snapshot total is 599,208,872.
method_rule: third aggregation error of this campaign, all the same shape: rank or sum without establishing the denominator. Print the total and the top entry's share of it; never sum a per-thread gauge as a per-process quantity.

method: scripts/dtrace/native-whole-cpu-budget.d, one cold go-build. profile-997 over the tracked tree, so samples/997 IS aggregate CPU-seconds -- the denominator every share is quoted against. Tracking is by carrick's own lifecycle USDT under `dtrace -Z` (`carrick*:::dsr-cache-capacity`), NOT by execname: execname is the binary basename and silently tracks nothing when the binary is renamed, which is what happens when comparing two built arms.
finding: Codegen is NOT the biggest bucket. DSR-inserted words are 18.6% of total CPU, not the ~30-40% the earlier census implied. The two largest buckets are user code OUTSIDE the JIT (36.9% -- carrick's own host text plus dylibs) and kernel time in NO syscall or mach trap (25.7% -- page-fault handling, with 1.71M zero-fill and 2.11M address-space faults). Together 62.6%. Guest instructions are 8.5% (3.51 CPU-s), which cross-checks against Docker's ~2.26 CPU-s for the same work.
bounds: 58% of user samples fell outside the JIT snapshots, so the 36.9% cannot be split between carrick host text, dylibs and non-JIT guest code from this run alone; the earlier range-classifier census split that population 16.8%/14.7%, implying carrick host ~20% and dylibs ~17%. The syscall on-CPU total varies run to run (4.12, 5.57, 6.12 CPU-s across three traced runs) because vtimestamp accounting is itself perturbed by tracing, so treat the syscall share as the softest number here and the sample-based splits as the firm ones.
consequence: Rank the next work off this table, not off the emitted-word census. Page-fault handling and carrick's host-side userspace are each larger than all inserted codegen, and neither has been attacked.

corrects: whole-cpu-budget-single-run-denominator, which claimed codegen was 18.6% and 'not the biggest bucket'. That rested on a SNAPSHOT-JOIN FAILURE: 58% of user PCs did not match any per-process JIT snapshot, and I read the unmatched population as host code. It was mostly JIT.
method: scripts/dtrace/native-user-module-split.d -- `umod(uregs[R_PC])` on every user-mode profile-997 sample. No snapshot join and no stack unwinding: addresses in no mach-o image ARE the MAP_JIT code cache. Tracking by lifecycle USDT under `dtrace -Z`.
finding: JIT is 52.9% of TOTAL CPU (75% of user), and the shape census puts 68.8% of JIT words in the DSR-inserted classes, so inserted codegen is ~36% of all CPU. Codegen IS the dominant bucket, which agrees with the ORIGINAL census (81.3% inserted of 37% JIT ~= 30%) and not with my erroneous 18.6%. carrick's own host text is 11.5% and all dylibs together 6.1%, so the 'attack carrick's userspace' direction the wrong reading suggested is worth about a third of what codegen is worth.
what_caught_it: A `profile-997` + `ustack()` run whose top 40 stacks covered only 2% of user samples, with 405 of 563 unsymbolized. A flat, unaggregatable distribution of user stacks is the signature of sampling inside a JIT: each PC yields its own garbage stack. That prompted the umod() split.
method_rule: For a user-side population, attribute by MODULE before attributing by symbol or by snapshot. `umod()` costs nothing, needs no unwind info and no side artifacts, and would have prevented both this error and the earlier assumption that unmatched snapshot PCs were host code.

mechanism_gate.residual_note: the 3.0% that remains is the accesses compact cannot take -- virtualized x18/x28 bases, stack-pointer bases, some writeback forms

prize: the bias load is 16.7% of JIT samples and JIT is 52.9% of total CPU, so removing 82% of it is worth about 7% of ALL CPU -- the largest single identified win left on this lane.
blocker: APERTURE_DISJOINT_ORR_BIAS carries an unfixed host-address leak, and the aperture FLAG lives in x18 in BOTH lowerings -- Darwin zeroes x18 asynchronously (~897/CPU-s), so a zeroing between the `lsr` and the second `cbz` lets a genuinely out-of-aperture access execute UNTAGGED against base+bias. That is pending task #14, and it is a latent gap in the SHIPPED lowering today, not only in compact.
consequence: Task #14 is no longer 'latent hardening'. It gates a measured ~7%-of-CPU win, which makes it the highest-value correctness work on the lane. Reverted the experimental candidate; do not ship the bias until the x18 flag dependency is gone.
design_note: Removing the x18 flag is not trivial: `cbz` on a shifted copy needs a scratch register, `tst`+`b.eq` writes NZCV which the lowering must not touch (`biased_fused_region_inserts_no_nzcv_writing_word`), and `tbz` tests only ONE bit so it cannot prove bits 41..63 are all clear for an arbitrary guest register value.
